stances.claim: China is correct that the SCS arbitral tribunal is 'totally different' from the International Court of Justice -- the ICJ is the UN's principal judicial organ, while the arbitral tribunal is constituted only under UNCLOS Annex VII for this particular dispute; further, the PCA itself did not render the decision but merely acted as the Registry, so calling the tribunal a 'PCA' decision is doubly inaccurate.
stances.rhetorical_move: partial-concession to opposing party + analytical-correction of common misattribution

stances.claim: The proper name of the deciding body is 'An Ad Hoc Arbitral Tribunal Constituted Under Annex VII of the 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea' -- and despite its temporary nature, its decisions are nonetheless binding on UNCLOS signatories like the Philippines and China.

The Philippines selected Judge Wolfrum (German), and when China declined to name a counterpart, the Itlos president appointed Judge Pawlak (Pole), then named three more -- Cot (France), Soons (Dutch), Mensah (Ghana, presiding) -- making the tribunal a multinational panel selected through procedurally proper UNCLOS mechanisms, not the 'puppet' body China alleges.

The PCA is not a court -- it is the Registry providing administrative services (transmitting communications, archiving documents, arranging fees, holding arbitration funds, providing Peace Palace hearing rooms) -- and has served as Registry in 11 of 12 arbitration cases filed under UNCLOS Annex VII, making the PCA's institutional role purely supportive rather than adjudicative.
stances.rhetorical_move: registry-not-court definitional distinction + institutional-frequency framing (11 of 12 cases)

notable_anecdotes: China's escalation pattern: refusal to participate → 'puppet' tribunal rhetoric → 'ill-grounded' award denunciation → ICJ-website citation to argue PCA inferiority -- capturing China's three-stage de-legitimization strategy.

CJ's partial concession to China's argument: 'I think China is correct in saying that the arbitral tribunal is totally different from the ICJ' -- a notable example of CJ acknowledging an opposing-party's correct technical claim even on a topic of high political stake.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban clarifies the institutional nature of the South China Sea arbitral tribunal -- distinguishing it from the International Court of Justice and the Permanent Court of Arbitration -- after China escalated its de-legitimization rhetoric following the July 12, 2016 Award that upheld most Philippine submissions and trashed China's nine-dash line. China, citing the ICJ website, argued the ICJ is 'totally different' from the PCA and that PCA arbitration lacks the sanctity of ICJ adjudication; CJ partially concedes that China is correct on the ICJ distinction (the ICJ is the UN's principal judicial organ; the tribunal is constituted only under UNCLOS Annex VII for this particular dispute) and adds that the PCA itself did not render the decision -- it acted only as the 'Registry.' The decision's own title, 'AN ARBITRAL TRIBUNAL CONSTITUTED UNDER ANNEX VII TO THE 1982 UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION ON THE LAW OF THE SEA' (capitalized in original), neither claims to be the ICJ nor the PCA, despite media and legal-expert mislabeling. After a stylebook digression on UNCLOS→'Unclos' (pronounceable abbreviation rule, contrasting with DOJ/all-caps), CJ explains Art 287(1)'s four dispute-settlement options for signatories: ITLOS (Hamburg), ICJ (The Hague), ad hoc arbitration under Annex VII, and special tribunal under Annex VIII; absent a stated preference, the default is ad hoc arbitration -- so the proper name is 'An Ad Hoc Arbitral Tribunal Constituted Under Annex VII of the 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea.' Though temporary, its decisions bind UNCLOS signatories like the Philippines and China. The tribunal was constituted June 21, 2013 with five members: Judge Rudiger Wolfrum (German, PH pick); Judge Stanislaw Pawlak (Pole, Itlos-appointed when China declined to name a member); Judge Jean-Pierre Cot (France); Prof. Alfred H. A. Soons (Dutch); and Judge Thomas A. Mensah of Ghana as presiding arbitrator -- a multinational, procedurally proper panel refuting China's 'puppet' characterization. The tribunal's Administrative Directive No. 1 appointed the PCA as Registry, with PCA senior legal counsel Judith Levine serving as registrar (rough equivalent of clerk of court). The PCA has acted as Registry in 11 of 12 Annex VII arbitration cases -- it is not a court but a service institution that transmits communications, archives documents, arranges arbitrator fees, holds arbitration funds, and provides Peace Palace hearing rooms.
